title: Chapter LIII

teacherSummary.text: Bingley returns to Netherfield and calls at Longbourn with Darcy. Mrs. Bennet is rude to Darcy and gushing to Bingley. Darcy is silent; Elizabeth is anxious.

context.history: Calls and returns of calls signal renewed courtship.

significance: Mrs. Bennet's rudeness to Darcy is ironic since he saved her daughter.
discussionQuestions: Why is Mrs. Bennet's rudeness ironic?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with marriage and money?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter LIII,” how does Austen show Bingley returns? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter LIII develops the idea of Bingley returns. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and plot shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter LIII to complicate the reader's understanding of Bingley returns. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter LIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of Bingley returns responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter LIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of Bingley returns. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: Why is Mrs. Bennet's rudeness ironic? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include fidgets, rekindled, intervene, witnessing, etiquette. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “Bennet was quite in the fidgets.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: To move uneasily one way and the other.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Calls and returns of calls signal renewed courtship. Now, why does this chapter matter? Mrs. Bennet's rudeness to Darcy is ironic since he saved her daughter. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Plot, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot characterization, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
segments.passage: But the spiritless condition which this event threw her into was shortly relieved, and her mind opened again to the agitation of hope by an article of news, which then began to be in circulation. The housekeeper at Netherfield had received orders to prepare for the arrival of her master, who was coming down in a day or two, to shoot there for several weeks. Mrs. Bennet was quite in the fidgets. She looked at Jane, and smiled, and shook her head by turns.
